title: Redwood Structured Output & Function Calling Demo - Cascade Retail
summary: AE + SE led demo focused on Redwood's structured output (JSON mode) and function-calling capabilities. Customer concerned about strict schema enforcement, escapes/invalid outputs, and private deployment (VPC) + KMS. Demonstrated console flow, API examples, schema validation, and guardrails (fallbacks, confidence scores). Agreed to run a short pilot: bench on 10k requests, share security docs and pricing. Next steps and owners recorded.
transcript:
[00:00] Alyssa: Hey everyone, uh, Cascade team, really appreciate you taking the time. I'm Alyssa Chen from Redwood — I'm the AE on the account. With me is Marco Ruiz, our SE, and Priya from product. Quick intro?
[00:12] Jordan: Hi, Jordan Lee — Head of AI at Cascade. Maya and Kevin on the line.
[00:18] Maya: Hey, Maya here, platform engineering.
[00:20] Kevin: Kevin, CISO.
[00:25] Alyssa: Great, quick agenda. We'll cover structured output JSON mode, function/tool calling, demos in the Console and API, then security and next steps. Marco will jump into the live demo. Sound good?
[00:35] Jordan: Yep, sounds good. Our main goals: strict schema adherence for our checkout assistant, deterministic fields for downstream systems, and of course latency/cost constraints.
[00:48] Marco: Perfect. So I'll share my screen — okay can you all see the Redwood Console? I'm in the model detail page, and we'll switch to the structured output tab. Note: sometimes the console labels show "Redwood Optima" on older builds, ignore that — it's Opti, um, a labeling quirk.
[01:10] [screen share noise, brief audio blip]
[01:20] Marco: Alright, first piece is JSON mode. We attach a schema — here is a simple order confirmation schema: order_id string, items: array of objects with sku, qty, price, total_amount number. We can set fields required and specify formats. When the model produces text we can validate, auto-correct and emit a confidence delta.
[01:42] Maya: When the model is off by a little, do you attempt to auto-cast strings to numbers? We had issues where price came out as "$12" and broke parsers.
[01:51] Marco: Yes, good question. We have three enforcement modes: "soft" (emit structured + raw, with validation flags), "strict" (reject/return error and optionally call a hinting tool), and "auto-cast" where common patterns are normalized — we try to strip currency symbols, parse numerics. You can configure at route or request level. Example in API: PATCH to /v1/responses with json_schema and enforcement=\"auto_cast\".
[02:21] Alyssa: Also worth noting, if strict mode rejects, Redwood can automatically fall back to a compatible model variant or call a custom repair function — Marco will demo that.
[02:31] Marco: Right — demo time. I'll run a prompt: 'Generate order confirmation for order 83A4, items...'. I'm toggling enforcement = strict to show behavior.
[02:40] [typing sounds]
[02:45] Marco: Ok sending.. and... we got a short-form: the model returned a partial JSON and then a trailing commentary, you can see the validator flags: missing total_amount and one item price is string. In strict mode the API returned 422 with validation_errors and the raw_text.
[03:05] Jordan: If that happens in prod, what's the recommended path? We can't have 422s breaking our event pipeline.
[03:12] Marco: Two options: (1) enable auto_repair hook (function-call) which invokes a repair tool we host or yours, runs a reformat step, and resends; or (2) routing fallback to a quantized but more stable model. You can configure retry policies in the route config with backoff.
[03:28] Maya: This repair tool — is it serverless? where does it run and how do we audit it?
[03:34] Marco: It can be either. Redwood supports function-calling to your service via an authenticated webhook, or you can use Redwood's built-in transform functions (runs in the platform sandbox). All calls are logged in the audit trail; you can also push logs to your SIEM.
[03:47] Kevin: What about PII? Any of these payloads stored in logs? We need to know retention and KMS behavior.
[03:53] Alyssa: Yes — good call, Kevin. For Hosted, we offer token-level retention controls and can disable retention. For Dedicated/Private we offer no retention by default. KMS integration for encryption at rest — we support customer-managed keys (AWS KMS, Cloud HSM options) and full audit logs. We'll send our SOC2 + architecture whitepaper after this.
[04:12] Marco: Back to demo — I'm switching to function calling. Here I've defined a schema for a function named 'createOrder' with args matching the order schema. The model can output a function call — e.g., {\"name\": \"createOrder\", \"arguments\": {...}} — and Redwood will optionally invoke the function or return the call payload to the client.
[04:36] Jordan: So Redwood can do the call for us? We're concerned about side effects if the model generates spurious calls.
[04:43] Marco: We have guardrails. First, you can require explicit confirmation in strict mode. Second, you can set allowed function whitelist per route. Third, we support a two-phase flow: model returns proposed call, you validate server-side and then execute. And we attach a confidence score + provenance header.
[04:58] Priya: For the provenance, can we see token ranges that triggered the call? That would help for audits.
[05:04] Marco: Yes, we include token-level spans and a trace id that links to the Console trace. Note — sometimes transcription of traces in older CE builds showed token ranges offset by one, it's a small index mismatch we've fixed in the last patch.
[05:18] [laughter]
[05:22] Marco: Now I'll demo a function-call flow with an injected bug: model suggests a negative qty. We'll show a pre-call validator rejecting it and returning a structured error.
[05:32] [typing] 
[05:40] Marco: Sending... Response: model proposed createOrder with item qty = -1. Pre-call validator rejected: violation 'qty must be >= 1'. The platform returned an error object and a suggestion: 'did you mean 1?'. This suggestion can be used in an auto-repair hook.
[05:56] Jordan: How does this impact latency? Our SLO for checkout completion is 300ms p95.
[06:03] Marco: Good question — structured output validation adds small CPU overhead. For hosted Redwood endpoints on dedicated pools we've seen median add of 20-40ms for schema validation + optional repair, p95 under 80ms depending on payload size. If ultra-low latency, you can precompile validation rules into the runtime (schema compiled) which reduces overhead. We can show benchmark numbers — I'll email the benchmark spreadsheet.
[06:26] Maya: Can we run this on our VPC? We can't have any egress to public infrastructure.
[06:31] Alyssa: Yes — Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem deployments. In that mode you can run the control plane privately and keep data on-prem. We also support dedicated capacity with no retention and customer-managed KMS.
[06:43] Kevin: Do you support SAML SSO + RBAC? We need team-based roles and audit exports.
[06:48] Priya: Yep — SSO (SAML/OIDC) and fine-grained RBAC is supported, audit exports to S3, and syslog/SIEM streaming. We'll attach the security checklist.
[06:59] Marco: Back to console — here's a route config where I set enforcement to auto_cast and register a repair function webhook URL. You can toggle per-route batching and quantization profile; Optimize will make recommendations based on token distribution.
[07:18] Jordan: Tell me more about Optimize — we saw a note in the docs.
[07:21] Priya: Redwood Optimize runs offline analyses of your prompt set and live traffic. It suggests batching windows, model variant (fp16 vs int8), and cache configurations. For example, for our retail use case the tool suggested a small prefix cache for product descriptions which reduced token usage 18% in one test.
[07:40] Maya: Any RLHF or safety layers integrated? We want to ensure hallucinations are minimized in order confirmations.
[07:47] Marco: Safety is multilayered: model choice, guardrail schemas, deterministic prompting patterns, and post-validation. For hallucination specifically, structured schemas plus required field checks remove a lot of downstream ambiguity. We also support evals and regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[08:03] [crosstalk — someone is interrupted]
[08:10] Kevin: One last security question — where do function webhooks leave the host network? We want to ensure egress is internal to our VPC.
[08:16] Alyssa: For Private deployments the function webhook can be an internal endpoint. For Hosted, Redwood will reach out from our control plane; we support IP allowlists and private peering options for sensitive callbacks.
[08:29] Jordan: Ok can we see an end-to-end demo — API call from their service, model returns function call, webhook executes createOrder and we see logs?
[08:37] Marco: Sure. I'll switch to the API tab and call the /responses endpoint live. I'll pass schema and a flag call_mode=\"execute\".
[08:47] [typing and CLI noise]
[08:52] Marco: Sent. The model returned function call, Redwood executed webhook, webhook returned 200 with order_id, and the Console trace shows the full timeline: model latency, validation, webhook latency. See the waterfall.
[09:07] Maya: Nice — what's the visibility retained in the Console? We need to show to product managers.
[09:12] Marco: You get per-request trace, token-level timing, validation flags, and the function payload. There's a link to download the raw event JSON. We'll share a sample link: https://app.redwood.ai/samples/trace/12345 (placeholder).
[09:26] Jordan: A couple of pragmatic items: (1) we need 99.9% uptime for business-critical checkout routes, (2) want to avoid model-churn surprises. How do you handle rollouts?
[09:36] Alyssa: Rollouts are in Console — canary percentages, auto-rollbacks on regressions (quality & latency), and label-based routing by region/tenant. We also keep old model versions archived so you can pin a stable variant.
[09:48] Jordan: Pricing — do we pay per-token? Any additional for function-calling?
[09:53] Alyssa: Hosted is per-token for generation/embeddings, plus per-call charges for function execution if Redwood executes the webhook. Dedicated is reserved capacity pricing. We'll share an indicative pricing sheet after this call.
[10:05] Priya: For the pilot we typically propose a 2-week PoC with 10k simulated requests across common prompts, plus one integration route into your staging webhook. It helps show latency and error rates.
[10:18] Jordan: Sounds good. One technical detail — do you support JSON Schema draft-07 or newer? We rely on certain features.
[10:25] Marco: We support draft-07 with many common extensions; for advanced validations you can plug in a custom validator in the repair function.
[10:34] [pause]
[10:38] Alyssa: Alright, quick recap before we wrap. Next steps: Alyssa will send security docs, Marco will share the benchmark sheet and a sample trace, and we'll schedule a 2-week PoC to run on staging. Cascade will provide a webhook endpoint and a representative set of 10-20 prompt templates.
[10:55] Jordan: I'll follow up with our procurement timeline — likely want a short MSA on top of the pilot.
[11:01] Kevin: We'll need SOC2 + pen test evidence before production.
[11:06] Alyssa: Absolutely — we'll include those artifacts. Anything else?
[11:10] Maya: One small ask — can you include an example of the repair hook code in Node and Python.
[11:15] Marco: Yep, will include.
[11:18] Alyssa: Thanks everyone, we'll send notes.
[11:22] [recording stops]
